I — Origins, 1844

A civil registry entry on an island of shipbuilders

The paper trail begins in Procida, a small island in the Bay of Naples, eleven years before the Kingdom that recorded his birth would cease to exist.

Page 1 — Declaration
Page 2 — Witnesses
Procida civil registry, entry no. 246, 1844 — the declaration, witnessed presentation, and naming of the child.
Enhanced crop — the father's domicile line, resolving to "domiciliato in Sant'Antonio."
Italian
English
Historical context

Num. d'ordine duecentoquarantasei. L'anno mille ottocento quarantaquattro il dì [1°?] del mese di Settembre, avanti di Noi Giovanni Ferrara[?], Uffiziale dello Stato Civile del Comune di Procida, Distretto di Pozzuoli, Provincia di Napoli, è comparso [nome del padre, poco leggibile], domiciliat[o] in Sant'Antonio, quale ci ha presentato un bambino... ed ha dichiarato che lo stesso è nato da Scotto di Quacquaro... Lo stesso ha inoltre dichiarato di dare al bambino il nome di Luigi.

Order number two hundred forty-six. In the year 1844, on the 1st of September, before Us, the Civil Registrar of Procida, District of Pozzuoli, Province of Napoli, there appeared [the father], residing in Sant'Antonio, who presented an infant and declared the child was born of Scotto di Quacquaro... The declarant gave the child the name Luigi.

The Kingdom that recorded him: in 1844 Procida belonged to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, the largest and oldest of the pre-unification Italian states, ruled from Naples by the Bourbon king Ferdinand II. This civil registry system — separate from church baptism — was itself a legacy of the earlier Napoleonic administration of the kingdom, carried forward by the Bourbons after 1815.

Sixteen years later: in 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand overthrew the Bourbon monarchy that had recorded Luigi's birth. By 1861 Procida belonged to the newly proclaimed Kingdom of Italy — the same political rupture that, within a generation, would help push men like Luigi toward the emigrant ships.

Why "Scotto di Quacquaro"? Compound surnames of the form "[Cognome] di [Toponym/Patronym]" are common across Procida and the wider Naples region — they emerged as a practical way to distinguish among the many families sharing a common surname like Scotto in a small island community. A parallel branch turns up later in these very records under a different qualifier — Scotto di Perto (see the "Tangent" note in the Legacy section below) — which is a useful illustration of exactly this naming pattern, not necessarily a sign of close kinship.

An island economy built on wood and water

Procida's 19th-century economy ran overwhelmingly on the sea. The island was one of the great wooden-shipbuilding centers of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies — local yards turned out merchant brigs and barques for Mediterranean and transatlantic trade, and a very large share of the men on the island worked as sailors, fishermen, shipwrights, or in trades that served those ships. A boy born in 1844 into that world — likely, given his adult trade, into a family with some connection to it — would have grown up around hulls, rigging, and the rhythms of a working port, whether or not any single record spells that connection out for us.

II — Marriage & First Child, 1878–1879

A wedding at the Abbey, a son on the island

The marriage record comes from the Abbazia di San Michele Arcangelo — the ancient Benedictine abbey that crowns Terra Murata, Procida's fortified hilltop old town, and the island's principal religious archive. Angelina, roughly eighteen at marriage, would have thirteen months later given birth to Raphael — the son who, four decades on, would become a Brooklyn banker witnessing dozens of his fellow Italians into American citizenship.

III — The Voyage, Winter 1880

Aboard the Anna Maria D'Abundo

No passenger manifest for Luigi's crossing has yet surfaced — a gap this section tries to explain rather than paper over.

The Anna Maria D'Abundo at anchor, photographed c. 1903 — a three-masted Italian barque of the type Luigi is believed to have crossed on in December 1880. Source: Royal Museums Greenwich ↗

Family naturalization and immigration records place Luigi's arrival at on or about 27 December 1880, aboard a ship he identified in later years as the Anna Maria D'Abundo. Contemporary shipping columns instead give her arrival as 23 December 1880 — close enough, across a five-day gap, to be the ordinary friction of memory versus a newspaper's dateline, rather than two different ships.

Contemporary confirmation: The New York Herald, Friday, 24 December 1880, "Marine Intelligence" column, recorded: an Italian barque named Anna Maria D'Abundo arriving from Palermo, having sailed on 5 November, carrying fruit and other cargo. This single newspaper line is currently the strongest independent corroboration of the crossing.

A barque, not a liner — what that means for the timeline

Unlike the steamships that dominate popular memory of Ellis Island (which, notably, did not open until 1892 — Luigi would have entered through Castle Garden, New York's earlier immigrant depot), the Anna Maria D'Abundo was a wooden, three-masted sailing barque. That made the crossing far slower and far more weather-dependent than the era's "nine-day" steamship passages:

01
Loading in Italy
3–4 weeks — fruit, olive oil, wine, passengers
02
Atlantic crossing
7–9 weeks under sail
03
Unloading in New York
2–3 weeks near South Street Seaport
04
Return + refit
6–9 weeks, incl. maintenance in Procida/Naples

Working backward from a 23 December arrival, a 45–65 day Atlantic crossing implies departure from Italy sometime between 20 October and 5 November 1880 — which lines up neatly with the Herald's own reported sailing date. If one-year-old Raphael really did travel with his father, as some immigration records suggest, this would have been his first transatlantic crossing of at least two in his lifetime.

Why this ship is a "ghost" in the archives

  • She was cargo, not a passenger liner. A barque hauling lumber, fruit, and oil was processed by customs cargo clerks, not immigration clerks — the paperwork trail is simply different from the one genealogists usually search.
  • Procida ran her like a family business. The D'Abundo family, who owned and captained ships of this name, sometimes listed travelers informally — as "friends of the captain" or supernumeraries on the crew list — rather than on a formal passenger manifest.
  • Smaller vessels were indexed differently. Databases built around the major lines (Cunard, White Star) often handle these Mediterranean-trade barques inconsistently, or not at all.

As of 2026, no manifest for this specific crossing has been located. This is treated here as an open research question, not a settled fact — see "Open Questions" below.

A Marseilles tangent: the customary route to New York in this period sometimes involved a stop in Marseilles. Family research notes record Scotto di Quacquaro names appearing in Marseilles-area genealogical archives — plausibly explained by travelers who fell ill mid-journey, stayed behind while the rest of the family continued on, and ultimately settled there rather than completing the passage. This is family tradition and pattern-matching from surname distribution, not a documented event tying directly back to Luigi — worth flagging as a lead, not a fact.
The D'Abundo family, briefly: the family whose name the ship carried was itself a Procida–Ischia maritime dynasty of real historical weight. 19th-century shipping registers list D'Abundo men as masters and owners of several vessels, and the name persists in Gulf of Naples shipping today through the modern ferry operator Medmar — whose fleet, fittingly, includes a vessel named Rosa d'Abundo. One notable 19th-century family member, Giuseppe D'Abundo (1860–1926), became a pioneering Naples-based neurologist, among the first to study the psychological effects of early cinema — a reminder that Procida's maritime families often had branches reaching well beyond the docks.
IV — Brooklyn Beginnings, 1882–1888

Three children, three City of New York certificates

All three birth certificates independently list Luigi's occupation as "Caulker" and his wife as Angelina, née Mazzella — the same names, the same trade, across six years.

Carmela · 1882
Celestra · 1883

Certificate of Birth, City of New York, No. 555 — NYC Historical Vital Records ↗
8 March 1882

Carmela Scotto di Quacquaro

Born at 107 Hamilton Avenue, Brooklyn. Luigi, age 36, occupation Caulker. Mother Angelina Scotto di Quacquaro (née Mazzella), age 22 — her second child, and the first born on American soil. Delivered by midwife Rachela Maresca of 60 President Street, who would go on to deliver both of Luigi's remaining recorded children.

Certificate of Birth, City of New York, No. 561 — NYC Historical Vital Records ↗
6 June 1883

Celestra (Celestrina) Scotto di Quacquaro

Same address, 107 Hamilton Avenue. Luigi now 37, still a Caulker. By this point the household held Angelina, four-year-old Raphael, one-year-old Carmela, and now Celestra — three living children in just over a year of documented Brooklyn life. Rachela Maresca again served as midwife, still residing at 60 President Street.

Certificate of Birth, City of New York, No. 557 (corrected) — NYC Historical Vital Records ↗
10 April 1888

Michele Liberato Scotto di Quacquaro

The family has moved to No. 1 Summit Street. Luigi, 42, still lists "Caulker" (recorded on the certificate in both English and its Italian equivalent, Calafate) — five years after Celestra's birth, and still the same trade. Angelina, 28, now with three previous children and four living. Rachela Maresca delivers again, still at 60 President Street.

A quiet cross-check: Luigi's stated ages on these three certificates — 36 in 1882, 37 in 1883, 42 in 1888 — back-calculate to a birth year of roughly 1845–1846, sitting close enough to the 1844 Procida birth record (allowing for the ordinary imprecision of self-reported age in this era) to support, though not prove outright, that these are the same man.

V — The Ship Caulker's Trade

Sealing hulls on the Brooklyn waterfront, 1880–1920

Caulking was a skilled maritime craft, not casual dock labor — and the distinction likely shaped everything that came after for this family.

Ship caulking involves sealing the seams of a wooden hull's planking to make it watertight — driving strands of oakum (hemp) or cotton into the seams with mallets and caulking irons, then sealing over them with pitch or tar. It was skilled, apprenticed work, tied to shipyards and dry docks rather than the day-to-day loading of cargo on the piers.

Procida's men — raised in a shipbuilding and seafaring economy — were well positioned to make this transition. A boyhood around hulls, planking, and pitch in the old country translated directly into employable skill on the Brooklyn waterfront, at a time when the Brooklyn Navy Yard in nearby Wallabout was one of the largest ship repair facilities in the world and a major employer of caulkers, carpenters, and shipwrights.

TraitLongshoremanShip Caulker
Skill levelLow–mediumHigh, apprenticed
HiringDaily "shape-up"Yard-based, steadier
Income stabilityErraticRelatively stable
Community statusWorking poorSkilled tradesman
Upward mobilityLimitedModerate
Reasonable inference, not documented fact: the steadier income, technical standing, and proximity to ship inspection and customs processes that came with skilled caulking work plausibly explain how Luigi's household — starting from a trade with more stability than casual dock labor — could support a son who moved from "Clerk, Groceries" in the 1900 census into banking, real estate, and community leadership within a generation. Direct causation between Luigi's trade and Raphael's rise can't be proven from the records in hand, but the pattern fits a well-documented feature of the era's waterfront labor economy: skilled tradesmen were more likely to become the translators, guarantors, and intermediaries their less-established neighbors relied on.
The padrone system, for context: many newly arrived Italians in this period found work — on docks, in construction, sometimes in shipyards — through padrones, informal Italian labor brokers who placed men in jobs in exchange for fees or a cut of wages. The system was often exploitative, but it anchored countless immigrants, including possibly Luigi himself in his earliest Brooklyn years, into trades they might not have accessed alone.
VI — Naturalized American, 1887

Twenty-one years off the boat, a citizen

Date21 October 1887
WitnessGiuseppe Mastello
Years since arrival≈ 7
Occupation on recordCaulker

Seven years after landing, Luigi became a U.S. citizen — a step that mattered practically (property ownership, voting, standing in court) as much as symbolically. It's a detail worth sitting with in light of what his son Raphael would go on to do: within two decades, Raphael himself would become one of the most-relied-upon naturalization witnesses for fellow Italian immigrants on Columbia and President Streets — a role that traces its plausibility straight back to Luigi's own naturalization, and to the standing that came with steady, skilled work and an early, settled address.

VII — Community & the Next Generation

From caulker's son to banker on Columbia Street

What survives most vividly in the archive isn't Luigi's own paper trail, but the institutions his son Raphael built on the foundation of it.

L. Scotto & Son — Brooklyn Daily Times, 28 Sept. 1912. Source ↗
"Society Antonia Scialoja" — Times Union (Brooklyn), 31 May 1901. Raphael Scotto listed as treasurer. Source ↗

By 1912, "L. Scotto & Son" — the "L." almost certainly standing for Luigi — operated as foreign and domestic bankers, steamship agents, and custom house brokers at 238 Columbia Street, with a branch office at 95 Navy Street, just blocks from the Navy Yard where so many caulkers found work. The firm's name preserves Luigi in the business even as Raphael ran it. A decade earlier, the Società Antonia Scialoja — a mutual aid and fraternal society with some 200 members marching in the 1901 Memorial Day parade, escorted by mounted police — had used Luigi's own home at 102 President Street as an early headquarters, with Raphael serving as treasurer.

A witness to dozens of new Americans

Naturalization petitions require character witnesses — established citizens willing to vouch for the petitioner. Raphael Scotto's name recurs across the surviving Brooklyn naturalization record as exactly that kind of witness, again and again, for men from across the Italian immigrant community:

One example of many — Pasquale Colella's 1903 naturalization card, witnessed by Raphael Scotto, 102 Pres. St., "Banker & Broker."
28 Mar 1903Francesco CammarotaLongshoreman · 74 President St
2 Apr 1903Luigi ForteLongshoreman · 67 President St
28 Mar 1903Pasquale ColellaLongshoreman · 76 Hamilton Ave
2 Jul 1904Raimondo CostagliolaCarpenter · 53 President St
1917Gaetano CaponeU.S. Army, WWI — sworn in at Binarville, France

Notably, Cammarota, Forte, and Colella were all longshoremen — the very trade caulkers stood a rung above — clustered on the same handful of streets as the Scotto family. Gaetano Capone's 1917 petition, sworn before a U.S. Army captain in wartime France, still named "Louis Scotto (Banker), 238 Columbia Street" as a character reference back home — a striking sign of how far this network's reach extended.

1939

Raphael Scotto, Real Estate

A short business letter survives from June 1939 — Raphael, by then styling himself simply "Real Estate, Brooklyn, New York," appraising a distressed mortgage property on Tompkins Place. A small, ordinary document, and a reminder that the family's Brooklyn story ran for decades past Luigi's own generation.

Tangent

The "Scotto di Perto" family

A 1904 birth certificate for Michele Salvatore Antonio Scotto Di Perto — son of Antonio Scotto di Perto and Elisabetta Scotto di Perto (née Manto), also delivered by Rachela Maresca, at 42 President Street — surfaces in the same records. Same street, same midwife, a similar compound surname pattern — but flagged here explicitly as an unconfirmed tangent, not a proven branch of Luigi's own family.

Reading Raphael's rise in context: Raphael's mentorship under Brooklyn power broker Anthony Sessa (whose own bank at 40 Union Street began as a grocery — a possible explanation for why 20-year-old Raphael was recorded as a "Clerk, Groceries" in the 1900 census, per family research notes), his marriage to Josephine Sessa, and his eventual part-ownership stake in the D. Costagliola Dry Dock and Shipyard together sketch a man building a vertically integrated position in the Procidan-Brooklyn community — banking, real estate, and shipping all under family control. This narrative is drawn from family research and newspaper record, and represents a plausible synthesis rather than an independently verified biography.
VIII — The Place

Sant'Antonio, Procida

The quarter named in the 1844 record still exists, still carries the same name, and is walkable in an afternoon.

40.7602° N, 14.0219° E Open in Google Maps ↗

Procida's nine grancìe

The island has long been divided into nine historic quarters — grancìe — each once tied to a parish or monastic estate. Sant'Antonio, Luigi's family quarter, is one of them.

1606

Chiesa di Sant'Antonio Abate

The quarter's namesake church, still standing near Via Cavour — the most direct physical link left to the neighborhood Luigi's father called home.

2022

Italy's Capital of Culture

Procida — long overshadowed by Capri and Ischia — was named Italy's Capital of Culture in 2022, drawing renewed attention to quiet, lived-in quarters like Sant'Antonio.

The Place, continued

The Brooklyn waterfront: Red Hook & Columbia Street

Every documented address for this family sits within a few blocks of the water — approximate pins below, for a future visit.

Columbia St / Red Hook, Brooklyn Open in Google Maps ↗

These pins are approximate, placed from historic street names rather than exact geocoded house numbers — Hamilton Avenue, Summit Street, President Street, and Columbia Street all still exist today in Brooklyn's Red Hook and Carroll Gardens neighborhoods, though numbering and some street configurations have shifted since the Brooklyn–Queens Expressway cut through the area in the mid-20th century.

Worth knowing before a visit: the Brooklyn Navy Yard — very plausibly where Luigi found steady caulking work — sits a few miles north along the same waterfront, and today operates as a working industrial park partly open to public tours.

IX — Open Questions

What the record hasn't given up yet

An honest accounting of the gaps, for whoever picks this research up next.

Is the passenger manifest for the December 1880 crossing findable?
Not yet located as of 2026. Best next steps: NARA cargo/customs records rather than immigration indexes, and Procida comune or Italian consular records that might list departing residents.
What was Luigi's exact hour and house of birth in Procida?
The 1844 register's ink is too faded on those specific lines to transcribe confidently — a sharper photograph of the original register would likely resolve this.
Is "Scotto di Perto" a related branch, or coincidence?
Currently unconfirmed. The shared street, shared midwife, and shared surname pattern are suggestive but not proof — worth a dedicated line of research.
When and where did Luigi die?
Not yet established in the notes this dashboard is built from — a natural next research target, likely in NYC Department of Health death records or Brooklyn cemetery archives.
Did Luigi work at the Brooklyn Navy Yard specifically?
Plausible given his trade and neighborhood, but not documented here — NARA Record Group 181 (Civilian Employment Cards, muster rolls, payroll ledgers) is the next place to check.
